newsitem.title: UK: Sumitomo probes grind on in U.S., Britain. [CORRECTED 18:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo probes grind on in U.S., Britain. [CORRECTED 18:45 GMT]

text.p: British and U.S. investigators have yet to finger anyone in the Sumitomo copper mystery as former star trader Yasuo Hamanaka goes on trial in Japan next week.
No conspiracies have been made public. No one has been arrested in Britain or the United States.
Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) launched its investigation last June on the day Sumitomo Corp rocked financial markets with news of losses that have reached $2.6 billion.
Probes by a U.S. Grand Jury and market watchdog soon followed.
The Japanese conglomerate said Hamanaka confessed to hiding a web of unauthorised deals and prosecutors arrested him last October.
In Britain, the world's hub for industrial metals trading, only a handful of raids have been announced but authorities insist investigations are on track.
Last week, the SFO was thrown off course when the agency itself was taken to court over a raid on a firm of accountants in connection with the Sumitomo case.
The High Court, however, ruled that the SFO was not in contempt of court for seizing computers and downloading data.
The agency added it could not say when the enquiry would be complete.
"Each case we handle is different...we are not in a position to speculate (when it will be finished)," the spokeswoman said.

One of the companies believed to be under scrutiny by the SFO is U.K.-based Winchester Commodities -- owned by multimillionaire ex-London Metal Exchange (LME) floor dealers Charles Vincent and Ashley Levett.
Press reports have said SFO searches of premises in Cornwall and Hampshire involved the homes of Vincent and Levett but the firm strongly denies any role in the Sumitomo losses.
"We have always said we are willing to cooperate with all enquiries and are happy to do so," a Winchester spokesman said.

Winchester, nevertheless, has been hit by the fall-out from the scandal. Its business is markedly down from 1995, when it was responsible for 14 percent of LME copper turnover of 17.24 million contracts.
In 1995 and 1996, respectively, both Levett and Vincent relinquished their directorships in the company they founded in 1991 and moved to Monaco.

In the United States, a probe by regulatory watchdog the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has focused on whether Hamanaka manipulated the copper market. New York's Comex futures market also trades copper.
Hamanaka faces no charge of market manipulation next week.

"Our investigation is continuing but it is premature to hazard a guess when that will be concluded," a CFTC spokesman said. The CFTC declined to comment on whether it would take part or be present at Hamanaka's trial.
The watchdog is also probing several U.S. banks engaged in derivatives transactions with Sumitomo, lending $1 billion to Hamanaka.
Attorneys and former regulators said a Hamanaka guilty plea could complicate the CFTC's task of trying to unravel the scandal.

The U.S. District Attorney's Office in Manhattan subpoenaed New York-based Global Minerals and Metals Corp for documents linked to its copper dealings with Sumitomo and Hamanaka. A Global spokesman said the company handed over the files last summer but has heard nothing since then.

In a separate move, a string of lawsuits filed by various U.S. traders alleging that Sumitomo, Hamanaka and Global Minerals and Metals (corrects to delete Birch Brokerage, which has been dismissed from lawsuit) manipulated the copper price are still being pursued, said Chris Lovell, the lawyer handling the cases. The lawsuits are set to be rolled into one and refiled soon, Lovell added.
Meanwhile, the LME has begun adopting reforms after a wide-ranging review by Britain's market watchdog, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB).
The watchdog told the LME, the world's centre for trade in industrial metals, to provide more information and tighten regulation in a December report.
